comparisons.peer_summary: In 2024, all four business units saw significant revenue increases: CNBU up 67% on higher bit shipments and DRAM ASPs, MBU up 75% from mobile DRAM and NAND ASPs and shipments, EBU up 27% driven by bit shipments despite lower ASPs, and SBU up 80% from higher ASPs and bit shipments.
comparisons.comparison: While both disclosures detail revenue performance by business unit or product mix, the trends are inversely correlated. Intel's CCG saw modest revenue growth (+4%) driven by volume recovery, whereas Micron's memory business units (CNBU, MBU, EBU, SBU) experienced massive revenue increases (27-80%) driven by significant rises in average selling prices (ASPs) and bit shipments. Intel's disclosure focuses on volume shifts and legacy exits in a mature market, whereas Micron's disclosure highlights a cyclical price and volume surge in memory, reflecting different stages of the semiconductor cycle for storage vs. logic/PC components.

comparisons.peer_summary: Compute & Networking revenue increased year-on-year, driven by a 266% growth in Compute due to higher shipments of the NVIDIA Hopper GPU computing platform for LLMs, recommendation engines, and generative AI, and a 133% increase in Networking due to higher InfiniBand shipments.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures attribute revenue changes to specific high-growth product shipments, but at vastly different scales and market contexts. Intel's CCG revenue increased 4% due to higher notebook volume, representing modest growth in the PC market. In contrast, NVIDIA's Compute & Networking revenue saw explosive growth, with Compute up 266% driven by Hopper GPU shipments for AI applications. This contrast highlights Intel's exposure to the more mature, volume-driven PC market versus NVIDIA's dominance in the rapidly expanding AI infrastructure market, where demand outstrips the modest PC recovery seen at Intel.
